title: How an LRU cache decides what to forget
subject: algorithm

scenes.why: Opening: state the question before showing any code.
scenes.title: How an LRU cache decides what to forget
scenes.subtitle: Twenty lines of Python and one ordered dictionary.

beats.say: A cache has limited room, so when it fills up, something has to go.
A least recently used cache makes that choice in the simplest way that works. It drops whatever you touched longest ago.

scenes.why: The claim is about what the code literally stores, so show the real lines.
scenes.heading: lru_cache.py · state

beats.say: The whole cache is one small class with two pieces of state.
A capacity, which is how many entries it may hold.
And an ordered dictionary, which remembers the order its keys were last touched. Oldest at the front, newest at the back.
beats.note: order of use is the whole trick

scenes.why: Entries change position over time; motion shows reordering and eviction better than any still.
scenes.heading: what the ordered dict is doing

beats.say: Picture that dictionary as a row of slots. The left end is the oldest entry, and the right end is the newest.
Reading a key, say A, counts as a use. So A jumps to the newest end, and the others shift down.
Now we add a fourth entry, D. It goes in at the newest end, and the cache is over capacity.
So the entry at the oldest end, B, is evicted. Not the first one we inserted, but the one we have ignored the longest.

scenes.why: Tie the animation back to the exact line that causes the jump.
scenes.heading: lru_cache.py · get

beats.say: Here is that read in code. A missing key just returns nothing.
A hit calls move to end. That one line is the jump you just saw.
beats.caption: A hit calls move_to_end. That one line is the jump you just saw.
beats.note: the jump to the newest end

scenes.why: put() is still the algorithm at work: the same row of slots, now driven by two decisions. Continuing the animation keeps one picture for the whole behaviour.
scenes.heading: what put() does

beats.say: Writing has two decisions in it. First, is this key already cached?
A is, so we mark it as newest, exactly like a read, and store the new value.
Second decision. Did that push us over capacity? Three entries, capacity three, so nothing is evicted.
But write a key the cache has never seen, and the row grows to four.
Now the check fails, so we pop the oldest end, and we are back within our limit.

scenes.why: Close the loop: the two decisions in the animation are these two if-statements.
scenes.heading: lru_cache.py · put

beats.say: And here are those same two decisions as code. Refresh the key if we already have it.
Then store, check the size, and evict from the front.

scenes.why: Recap: three claims the viewer should leave with.
scenes.title: What to remember
items: Order of use lives in one ordered dictionary
Every read and write moves a key to the newest end
Over capacity? Drop the oldest end

beats.say: So, three things to remember. The order of use lives in a single ordered dictionary.
Every read and every write moves a key to the newest end.
And when the cache is over capacity, it drops the oldest end. That is all least recently used means.
